description: I’m interested in space, AI, and building practical solutions with NASA data. I’m looking for curious teammates with skills in coding, design, data analysis, or storytelling. Let’s learn together and build something meaningful!
summary:
We created Spacefire Explorer, a web app designed to help researchers and spacecraft designers find and compare NASA combustion experiments related to fire safety in space.
Users can choose a spacecraft preset and adjust conditions such as oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity, and fuel type. The app then ranks relevant experiments using a transparent scoring system, allows users to compare studies side by side, and provides links to the original NASA sources.
So far, Spacefire Explorer includes 24 investigations and 1,984 individual test records. The app also highlights areas where data is limited, such as combustion experiments under Martian gravity.
Our goal is to make NASA's research easier to explore and use. Instead of searching through hundreds of experimental records, researchers and designers can quickly see which findings are relevant to their spacecraft and where more testing is needed.
We believe this is important because understanding what we already know, and what we still don't, can help teams make better decisions about fire prevention, detection, and suppression on future space missions.
details:
What it does and how it works

We built Spacefire Explorer, a web app that makes it easier to explore NASA's research on spacecraft fire safety. Users start by choosing one of five spacecraft environments: ISS, Moon Base, Pressurized Rover, Mars Base, or Spacesuit. They can then adjust conditions such as oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity, and fuel type.

Based on these settings, the app ranks relevant studies with a score from 0 to 100. Users can click "Why?" to understand how each score was calculated, compare two experiments side by side, and access the original NASA records.

Data and tools

We used data from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database and the NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS).

We built the dashboard using JavaScript and used Python to clean and validate the initial BASS-II dataset. The web app is hosted on Vercel. We also integrated Google Gemini for optional "Ask" and "Explain" features, which help users understand the research without having to go through every record themselves. To keep the answers reliable, our server checks that the citation IDs match the NASA records provided to the model.

What makes it creative

One of the main features of Spacefire Explorer is its interactive 3D room, which helps users connect a proposed spacecraft environment with real experimental data.

For example, when users select Moon Base, the app compares its preset oxygen concentration of 30% with 134 solid-fuel experimental runs. The highest oxygen concentration measured in those runs was only 22.2%. This makes it easy to see where existing research may not fully represent the conditions of a future Moon habitat.

Users can also explore individual data points on the chart and export the original test records as CSV files for further analysis.

Benefits and impacts

One of the challenges with spacecraft fire-safety research is that experiments are often carried out under very different conditions. Results from one experiment may not directly apply to another spacecraft environment.

We wanted to make these differences easier to understand. Spacefire Explorer helps users see how oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, and fuel affect the relevance of each study. It also highlights where experimental data is missing or limited.

For example, under zero gravity and Martian gravity settings, the app hides its illustrative flame visualization and warns users that the PSI data included in our catalog does not provide direct flame measurements for those conditions.

Our goal is not to replace scientific testing, but to make existing research easier to find, compare, and understand. We hope Spacefire Explorer can help mission teams make more informed decisions about fire prevention, detection, and suppression, while also identifying areas where further experiments are needed.
